title: Ansel and the Protocol
premise: August Yarrow has spent eleven years alone on Kepler Station, tending a seed-vault garden for colonists who will never arrive and maintaining a beacon whose original orders were lost in the war. When the ship Meridian returns from deep space carrying a crew aged backward into children, August learns the beacon is actually a dead-man's switch: if it goes silent, both warring factions will interpret it as an attack and launch. To stop the countdown, August and the Meridian's youngest-again captain, Ilsa Voss, must physically carry the beacon's true message — proof that the war's first strike was engineered by their own command — across contested space to the armistice council, while the station reactor runs toward meltdown. They deliver it at the cost of the garden and nearly themselves; the truth ends the war, but only because August chooses to broadcast it openly rather than trade it for power.
about_author: Noor Underhill is a former hydroponics technician who writes science fiction about people who maintain things nobody thanks them for. Ansel and the Protocol is her third novel, written in a converted greenhouse on the Atlantic coast.

chapters.title: The Garden for No One
chapters.summary: August's POV. A day in the routine of Kepler Station: pruning wheat lines, logging the beacon pulse, talking to seedlings as company. Establishes loneliness worn like a uniform. Emotional beat: quiet devotion masking grief over the colony that never came.

chapters.title: Signal in the Dark
chapters.summary: August detects an approaching ship broadcasting no registry. Hope and dread collide — the first human contact in four years. Emotional beat: trembling anticipation, the fear of wanting something again.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.summary: The ship docks; its crew are children wearing adult-rated suits. August meets Captain Ilsa Voss, now twelve years old, still giving orders in a voice that hasn't changed. POV alternates August/Ilsa. Emotional beat: uncanny recognition between two people who should be strangers.

chapters.title: Aged Backward
chapters.summary: Ilsa explains the deep-space jump anomaly: time ran backward aboard Meridian. The crew remembers the future of the war but not how to tie their boots. August realizes the beacon may have caused or recorded it. Emotional beat: vertigo and reluctant partnership.

chapters.title: Orders Nobody Wrote
chapters.summary: Digging through station archives, they find the beacon's original commissioning — redacted by fleet command itself. August's sense of purpose curdles into suspicion. Emotional beat: betrayal by an institution that was never there.

chapters.title: Children of the War
chapters.summary: Ilsa's crew struggles: a chief engineer of six years old, a doctor who can't reach the top shelf of her own medbay. August teaches them to live while they work. Emotional beat: tenderness growing where duty used to be.

chapters.title: The Dead-Man's Switch
chapters.summary: They decode the beacon: silence triggers mutual retaliation protocols on both sides. Worse, the reactor that powers it is failing — the countdown begins whether anyone fires or not. Emotional beat: cold clarity; the stakes become mechanical and merciless.

chapters.title: What Ilsa Remembers
chapters.summary: Ilsa confesses what future-Meridian learned before the jump reversed them: the war's opening strike was ordered by their own high command to seize the beacon technology. She carries the proof in her memory — literally encoded in her restored neural pattern. Emotional beat: the burden of being evidence.

chapters.title: Two Flags
chapters.summary: Both factions detect the beacon fluctuation and dispatch ships. August must choose which side to hail; either choice looks like defection. First hostile contact. Emotional beat: the impossibility of neutrality once you're seen.

chapters.title: Ansel
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter to August's training years and the mentor, Ansel Okonkwo, who taught him that maintenance is a moral act — and who disappeared after questioning command. His name is all over the beacon's code. Emotional beat: inheritance, and the question of what loyalty really means.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Fleet Admiral Serrano hails August personally: restore the beacon, hand over Ilsa's memory, and be rewarded with the colony he was promised. Power dangles belonging. Emotional beat: temptation dressed as homecoming.

chapters.title: Grafting
chapters.summary: A quieter chapter: August and Ilsa graft new stock in the garden, and something like love — or its beginning — takes root between two people out of sync with time. Emotional beat: warmth stolen from a burning clock.

chapters.title: Mutiny of the Small
chapters.summary: The child crew votes: they will not be handed to either flag. Ilsa leads them in seizing Meridian's systems back from remote fleet lockout. Emotional beat: fierce solidarity from the least powerful people in the system.

chapters.title: Reactor Breach
chapters.summary: The station reactor destabilizes ahead of schedule; evacuation means abandoning the beacon mid-countdown. August stays behind to stabilize it manually while the children launch. Emotional beat: sacrifice framed as simple maintenance.

chapters.title: Burn Rate
chapters.summary: Alone in the radiation-shielded core, August buys hours with his own exposure. Interleaved with his fading logs, we learn Ansel didn't vanish — he was erased for building this very failsafe. Emotional beat: communion with a ghost through code.

chapters.title: The Chase Through the Shoals
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Meridian threads the debris shoals with two warships closing in, flown by a crew whose bodies can't withstand combat g-forces. Improvisation over firepower. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into audacity.

chapters.title: Serrano's Truth
chapters.summary: Cornered, Ilsa broadcasts a fragment of her memory openly. Serrano's own officers hesitate; some defect. The admiral pivots from suppression to spin. Emotional beat: power showing its cracks when truth becomes contagious.

chapters.title: Countdown Zero
chapters.summary: Climax part one. The beacon hits critical silence threshold as August, half-blinded, makes the choice Ansel built the switch for: instead of restoring the old protocol, he replaces it — broadcasting Ansel's full archive and Ilsa's testimony to every receiver in the system. Emotional beat: love against duty resolved into a third thing — witness.

chapters.title: Ceasefire at Kepler
chapters.summary: Both fleets hold fire as the transmission lands. Serrano attempts one last strike and is arrested by her own bridge crew. The war doesn't end neatly; it simply stops being able to justify itself. Emotional beat: exhausted, disbelieving relief.

chapters.title: What the Garden Cost
chapters.summary: Rescue teams find August alive but changed; the garden is scorched except one wheat line. Ilsa and the crew return to a station that belongs to no faction now — a neutral ground by accident and by choice. Emotional beat: mourning braided with gratitude.

chapters.title: Planting Season
chapters.summary: Months later: the armistice council ratifies the Kepler Accords. Colonists finally come — not the ones August waited for, but real ones. He plants the surviving wheat line in open ground. Emotional beat: belonging earned rather than promised.

chapters.title: The Beacon Keeps Time
chapters.summary: Final chapter, August's POV. The beacon now broadcasts the archive continuously — a lighthouse of truth rather than a tripwire of fear. August and Ilsa watch the first settler children run through the garden. Emotional beat: peace as an ongoing act of maintenance, never finished, always tended.
